title: How to Stop Scammers From Showing You Ads on Your Android After Every Phone Call
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're an Android user who is seeing ads pop up after your phone calls, you need not assume this is some new feature you have to learn to live with. It's actually an ad fraud scam, and you can do something about it. Researchers have identified dozens of apps on the Google Play Store that are able to display ads on top of the Android phone interface, a scheme known as AfterCall. How ads are taking over Android callsThis scam originates with seemingly harmless utility apps downloaded from the Google Play Store, such as calendars, alarm clocks, and notepads. When installed, they request overlay permissions, which allow them to appear on top of other apps—and thus display ads over phone calls. These apps can detect when a call ends and will then launch full-screen ads wrapped in a fake call info screen. Since it looks like they are simply part of the call interface, users may be less likely to suspect that they are actually malicious. It's worth noting that overlay permissions can't be granted via a standard pop-up during the app installation process. They are a type of "special permission" that requires users to go into their system settings to enable. Android apps are supposed to request these permissions in context and give a clear reason for doing so. AfterCall scammers are using justifications like alarms not being able to go off or appear correctly without overlay permissions, though some apps will simply crash if users decline permissions.
How to remove AfterCall adsBecause the ads appear out of context—after a phone call and with content unrelated to the utility app—it's harder for users to figure out what's causing them. The utility apps aren't obviously malicious and don't appear on recent app lists when ads are displayed, so it's not obvious that they are connected to the problem. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you are seeing ads pop up after phone calls on your Android, check for apps that have overlay permissions. Go to Settings > Apps > Special app access (this may be hidden behind a three-dot menu) and click on the permission type. Look for apps you don't recognize, or which shouldn't have "display on top" permissions, and uninstall them. You should regularly audit these permissions, and disable any that aren't essential. On the user side, these apps seem to be mostly an annoyance rather than outright malicious programs that are harvesting your sensitive data, though installing any program that requests unnecessary permissions can introduce significant risk. If nothing else, however, these apps do appear to waste brands' advertising dollars and could damage their reputation with users—but you probably just care about how to stop seeing them after your calls.

title: It Just Got a Lot Cheaper to Try Gemini Spark, Google's AI Agent
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gemini Spark, the AI agent built into Google Gemini, is now a lot cheaper to try out in the U.S. Previously, Gemini Spark was exclusive to the Google AI Ultra plan, which costs $100-$200 per month. The company is now bringing the agentic AI to its AI Pro plan, which costs $20 per month. (For now, this change is exclusive to the U.S.)When Gemini Spark was announced during Google I/O 2026, its features seemed potentially useful, but the barrier to entry was too high for most people. That appears to be changing now, as Google has cut the price by as much as 90%. It is not yet available on the $5/month AI Plus plan or the free tier, but that could change in the future too—though it's likely that using Gemini Spark on lower pricing tiers could mean that you hit your usage limits much faster.What is Gemini Spark?Google Gemini is a chatbot and a voice assistant that answers your questions, creates text, media, and even entire apps for you. Gemini Spark takes those capabilities to your Google account and executes actions for you.
You can think of Gemini Spark as a personal AI assistant that can look at your emails, calendar entries, photos, and other data in your Google account to perform tasks on your behalf. You can use Spark to bulk unsubscribe from mailing lists, make flight bookings, send reminder emails to clients, colleagues, or family members, book appointments, and much more. Having said all that, a Gemini Spark overview from out sister site PC Mag emphasizes that its features tend to overlap with Gemini. PC Mag called Spark the best AI agent yet, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Does Gemini Spark respect your privacy?To someone who is even remotely privacy-conscious, using Gemini Spark is going to sound quite invasive: You basically have to give it access to your entire computer if you want it to be able to act on your behalf. Google is aware of that, and has programmed the AI agent to ask for confirmations before performing certain actions. If you ask the agent to find birthday photos from 2017 and email them to someone, for example, Gemini Spark will show you the pictures and ask for a confirmation before actually sending the email. It applies the same logic to deleting emails, sending messages, using your saved credit cards to pay for reservations, and more.It's worth keeping in mind that AI services have created serious problems for people who use these apps without due caution. The biggest strength of Gemini is its access to all the data that’s in your Google account, but if you give it unrestricted access and the AI agent messes up a request, you could be stuck with an incorrect hotel reservation, a flight booked to a wrong country, or other serious consequences.

T-Mobile has not made a public comment about the outage so far, but its Help account on X is responding to user complaints with boilerplate responses. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

The company claimed the outage did not stem from a cyberattack, rather a software issue. We don't know why T-Mobile is down at the moment, but, in all likelihood, the company will update the public sooner than later, if not fix the issue altogether.

title: Scammers Are Impersonating Spotify to Steal Your Credit Card Info
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: 	Chris McGrath / Getty Images News via Getty Inages
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Scammers love to impersonate trusted brands—ranging from big tech names like Microsoft and Google to password managers and payment apps—in their phishing campaigns to lure their marks, and their latest guise is Spotify. A new email is circulating alerting users to supposed payment issues, prompting them to hand over their credit card details and Spotify login credentials. Phishing emails use Spotify brandingAs The Guardian reports, Spotify users have received messages with the subject line "review billing info" claiming that the platform "encountered an issue while processing your recent payment." Recipients are urged to "review and update" their information to keep their accounts active. The button in the email directs users to a spoofed website, where users are prompted to enter their username and password, followed by their credit card number, address, and phone number—everything scammers need to make fraudulent purchases. One victim reported seeing a suspicious charge for more than $600 within minutes of handing over their information. The emails closely replicate Spotify's branding, including its colors and logo, and appear to come from a sender called MySpotify. The fraudulent website also looks convincing at first glance. However, unlike some of the more sophisticated phishing schemes that exploit vulnerabilities in order to use real domains (like Google and PayPal), this one from Spotify breaks down when you look closer. 
For one, both the sender's address and the website URL clearly are not connected to spotify.com or any legitimate subdomain. The subject line is all lowercase, and there are no specifics about users' subscriptions or accounts in the email body. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to avoid getting scammed by Spotify impersonatorsPayment issues are a common scam tactic, and you should always be skeptical of any communication that urges you to provide or update banking or credit card info (or sends you to a login page along the way, which is designed to harvest your credentials). If you receive a notification from Spotify about failed payments, don't click links, download attachments, or reply. Spotify won't request payment info, passwords, or other sensitive information over email.If you're concerned about a payment or subscription problem, go directly to your account in the Spotify app or a web browser instead. If you've already entered your Spotify credentials into a suspicious site, change your password and keep an eye on your credit card transactions to catch any fraudulent charges. You can also forward phishing emails to [email protected].

title: Google Docs Is Rolling Out These Three New Gemini Features
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 30, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google is rolling out new Gemini features in Google Docs for select users.
                                            Gemini can now generate and edit images directly in Google Docs, pulling from the context of your doc.
                                            Gemini can also generate and edit multiple images at once, based on the prompt.
                                            The features are rolling out now to Workspace users, including Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subcribers.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google makes both Gemini and Docs, so it's not surprising that you'll find plenty of the former's features while using the latter. Gemini has a ton of Google Docs integration, including reading your text out loud, searching and summarizing your Docs in Drive, and a "Gemini bar" embedded into the app for prompting anytime. It's to the point that it's tough to avoid, which isn't great news for Google Docs users uninterested in AI features. Of course, that won't stop Google. The company continues to add new Gemini features at a steady clip, and this week is no exception. As Android Authority notes, Gemini is now rolling out new image creation and editing abilities available directly in Google Docs. Google announced the changes in a Workspace update on Tuesday, highlighting how Docs users can tap into Gemini to create and edit images, diagrams, and infographics in their documents. According to Google, Gemini has three new functions Workspace users can take advantage of. First, users can create infographics or diagrams that summarize the doc in question. You could ask Gemini to do something like "add a diagram that explains the proposal at the top of this doc," or "create an infographic that summarizes the doc visually." Google says Gemini will pull from the context of the doc for these graphics, so these images should reflect what you have written in your doc—excluding the odd hallucination, of course.
In addition, Gemini can "refine existing visuals." You can ask Gemini to adjust the images in your doc with requests like, "change the aspect ratio of this image to 4:3," or "match the image's style to the other images in this doc." Finally, you can also ask Gemini to generate or edit multiple images at once. You could request the AI to create infographics in each section of your doc, or update all images at once.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Who has access to these new Gemini features?These new additions to Google Docs aren't rolling out to everyone. Instead, they're exclusive to Workspace users, which includes Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. If you pay for Google's AI features, you can try these out once they roll out on your end. If your school, work, or organization uses Workspace, the same applies. Here's the full list:Business: Business Standard and PlusEnterprise: Enterprise Standard, and PlusEducation: Education PlusConsumer: Google AI Pro and UltraEducation Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education; Teaching and Learning

title: Google Is Rolling Out a Video-Selfie Option If You Get Locked Out of Your Account
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google is adding a new video selfie sign-in option for user accounts.
                                            You can use it for identity verification if you're having trouble logging in.
                                            The feature seems to be available for some but not all users right now.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Finding yourself locked out of your Google account for whatever reason is a stressful situation to be in—what with all your emails, documents, photos, and other data suddenly out of bounds—but there's now a new way to prove your identity and regain access: a simple selfie video.It's always wise to have multiple sign-in methods set up, beyond the basic password and email address, as each additional one gives you a better chance of getting your account back if something goes wrong. The recovery contacts feature is a good example, where Google uses verified, trusted contacts of yours to prove your identity.Now you can also use a selfie video. By following this link you can see if the feature is live for your account, and record your selfie via a webcam or phone camera. If you're having trouble logging in, you'll be able to record a new selfie, which will be compared against the original saved in your account.
At the moment, the selfie video option for my account isn't available, so I couldn't test it out. It seems this will be rolled out gradually to users, though Google hasn't said anything specific about availability or a schedule—just that users can now check if their account is eligible."Your selfie video is yours and you're in control," says Google in its announcement blog post. "It is recorded and securely stored with your consent, and you can delete it at any time in your Google Account. It's used only for helping you sign in, unless you opt to share it for additional purposes. Your selfie video is encrypted at rest, meaning it's securely stored even when it's not being used."Those "additional purposes"  mean that Google will use your "video and related data to help ongoing efforts to develop and improve facial recognition, age estimation, and other verification methods that may use your physical features or movement" (the specter of age verification looms large again).
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There's also the rather obvious issue of deepfakes. Google says there are "multiple layers of security" to guard against fake photos and videos, including getting you to go through several simple movements when recording the selfie—movements that are hard to predict and mimic with a deepfake.All of the usual Google account checks will be in force too, so (for example) you might find additional security questions pop up if you're suddenly trying to log in from the other side of the world from where your usual login attempts are.Given the accuracy of technologies like Face ID these days, video selfie sign-in should prove to be a useful backup method of accessing your account. There's nothing extra for you to remember—you just have to bring your face—and it appears at the moment to be difficult to get around.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Facebook is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark.
                                            This is a separate feature from Meta Verified, which is a paid subscription for obtaining a blue check mark in Facebook and Instagram.
                                            You'll record a short selfie video, which Facebook will compare to other profile photos, but you should consider whether you want to provide more data to Meta.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. How Facebook Verified worksFacebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. 
Consider your privacy firstFacebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: 10 Hacks Every Google Sheets User Should Know
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: René Ramos/Lifehacker/Google/Adobe Stock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you don't spend hours every day working in spreadsheets, you may know only the basics of what Google Sheets can do: add, subtract, and sort data. But Sheets has a lot of powerful features that make data management simpler for even the casual user. Here are 10 hidden Google Sheets tricks everyone should know. One of the best features of Sheets and other Google Workspace apps is that collaborators can make and view changes in real time. In some cases, though, you may not want to share your live spreadsheet, instead providing a clean copy or a downloadable CSV. With editable sharing links, you don't need to make copies or export manually. Simply replace /edit at the end of the link with /copy (for a clean duplicate) or either /export?format=pdf or /export?format=csv (for file downloads). Create cell links to direct collaborators to specific cells or data blocksWhen you want collaborators to review a specific part of a large dataset, you don't need to provide a cell number or range for them to find manually. Instead, send them a link directly to an individual cell or cell block. Highlight the cell or cell range, right-click, and select View more cell actions > Get a link to this cell/range. The link will be copied to your clipboard so it can be easily shared. 
Create in-cell mini charts in Google Sheets to see trendsSheets has powerful data visualization features, but if all you need is a simple trend line, you can do that within a cell for an at-a-glance look at data over time. This also keeps your spreadsheet clean, so you don't have multiple charts and graphs overlaying the rest of your data. Type =SPARKLINE into a cell, select your range, and hit Enter. Apply conditional formatting’s custom gradients to see high and low values at a glanceConditional formatting applies colors to your cells based on specific rules—for example, color-coding project statuses or deadlines based on due dates or turning negative currency amounts red while positive amounts display green. An extra layer of conditional formatting is custom gradients, which shades values based on a scale so you can see high and low ends of the range at a glance. To set this up, go to Format > Conditional formatting > Color scale and select the cell range, min and max values, and color gradient. Then press Done. Use Smart Chips to insert interactive elements and Drive files for live collaborationSmart Chips are interactive, clickable elements in Google Workspace that allow you to tag contributors, link files, insert tables or status dropdowns, or quickly add dates and emojis to your spreadsheet. When you add a Drive file, for example, clicking the cell will pull up a preview of and link to the document, which is far cleaner than copying and pasting the full URL. Simply type "@" into any cell to pull up the Smart Chip menu. Set up custom terms and dropdown shortcuts in Sheets to simplify typed inputsWhile Sheets doesn't have the same native text substitution feature as Docs (allowing you to set up shortcuts that automatically turn into longer text), there is a workaround using dropdowns. This way, you can quickly add longer inputs that you frequently find yourself typing out and formatting, such as addresses, phone numbers, category labels, and brand names. Go to Insert > Dropdown and enter the text you want to appear in the Option box. You can add multiple choices and color code them as well. (Alternatively, you can use the Smart Chip hack above and select Dropdown from the menu.) Another text tweak in Sheets and across Workspace is the personal dictionary, which keeps Google from marking words as spelling errors. Add brand-specific terms, names, and other commonly used words and phrases via Tools > Spelling > Personal dictionary. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use IMPORTHTML to scrape and auto-refresh web data If you want to pull publicly available data into your spreadsheet but don't want to go through the potentially tedious process of copying, pasting, and reformatting, use the IMPORTHTML command to have Sheets do all of that for you. Paste =IMPORTHTML("url", "query", "index") and fill in the URL of the page you want to pull from, whether it's a "table" or "list" in the query field, and the table number on the live page. The data refreshes each time you open or refresh your spreadsheet, so you don't have to update them manually. Note that this function only works on public websites that don't require a login to access. Turn on data cleanup to remove duplicates and extra spaces from raw data importsIf you do need to import raw data from external sources (like CSVs) into your spreadsheet, Sheets can take care of some of the cleanup, so you don't have to manually remove duplicates from a huge dataset. Go to Data > Data Cleanup and select from Remove duplicates, Trim whitespace, or Cleanup suggestions. Link your spreadsheet to a Google Form to organize responsesGoogle Forms feed responses into Sheets, but you can also go in reverse and link a new form to your existing spreadsheet. For example, within your master budget spreadsheet, you can create a new tab for each month, and then use a Google Form with basic questions like transaction date, amount, and expense type to submit charges that autopopulate back to that tab instead of dealing in the spreadsheet directly. Go to Tools > Create a new form. This will pull up a form response tab in your spreadsheet (which can be renamed for the specific month) and an editable Google Form. Note that you'll need to publish the form in order to use it. If you have Workspace AI features, you can also have AI generate the form for you. Use Google Translate commands to quickly translate cell contentsSheets has a built-in Google Translate function, which allows you to convert text from one language to another without copying and pasting into another tool. Use this when you travel to create a dynamic, side-by-side phrase dictionary or apply it to a Google Form feedback sheet that receives inputs in multiple languages. Paste the command =GOOGLETRANSLATE(cell, "auto", "target_language") in which "auto" is the current language ("en" for English, for example). Then, highlight and drag across the row or down the column as needed.

title: iOS 26.6 Comes With Two New Features, and One Is Key for iOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 27, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Trutschel / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's next update isn't iOS 27: it's iOS 26.6, which the company rolled out to compatible iPhones on Monday.
                                            The update comes with two features you need to know about, one of which makes it possible to use Siri AI immediately after installing iOS 27.
                                            The other sends you an alert after you've blocked too many contacts on your iPhone, though that exact limit appears unclear.
                                            Finally, iOS 26.6 comes with a series of security updates.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        When you think about a big iPhone update on the horizon, iOS 27 likely comes to mind. And yet, Apple just released a totally different update: iOS 26.6. Typically, iOS updates this close to the launch of the next major version are focused on security fixes and squashing bugs, saving any major changes for the next big numbered update. And while iOS 26.6 comes with these under-the-hood adjustments, it also comes with two new features you should be aware of—including one that actually lays the groundwork for iOS 27.Preparing your iPhone for Siri AIiOS 26.6's first feature won't reveal itself when you install the update on your iPhone. In fact, most of us may think iOS 26.6 has no new features at all. But the update's most important new change is key for compatible iPhones upgrading to iOS 27. As it turns out, iOS 26.6 "optimizes the Spotlight index" on your iPhone to prepare it for iOS 27. In other words, the update gets your iPhone ready for Siri AI. Apple's AI-powered assistant relies on the new search architecture in iOS 27 to run properly. As such, if you install iOS 27 without updating to iOS 26.6 first, it may take days before Siri AI can perform as expected. By preparing your iPhone with iOS 26.6 now, you'll avoid the growing pains.
Of course, that won't benefit everyone eventually upgrading to iOS 27. While the update runs on iPhone 12 and newer devices, only the iPhone 15 Pro and newer can try Siri AI. Still, if that's you, iOS 27's new Siri will run much more smoothly coming from iOS 26.6 than from iOS 26.5.2.     iOS 26.6's other new feature is a new alert, letting you know that you've reached iOS' limit of the number of contacts you can block. It's not clear exactly how many contacts that is, but new code in the update confirms the alert is present. The alert reads: "Blocked Contacts Limit Reached: You’ve reached the maximum number of blocked contacts. To block additional callers, remove a blocked contact in Settings."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The thing is, there's no documentation of what that limit actually is. In fact, anecdotal evidence suggests that the limit is user-dependent. MacRumors reports that some users receive the alert after blocking 20,000 contacts, while others only get 8,000. I've seen comments suggesting the limit is lower still, with some claiming to hit it in the 5,000s. Nonetheless, that's a lot of blocked contacts, and will likely only apply to users who receive an overwhelming number of calls and messages from unwanted sources. iOS 26.6's security updates and bug patchesLike most of Apple's updates, iOS 26.6 comes with a series of security patches to fix vulnerabilities discovered since the last update—a large number of patches, at that. iOS 26.6 includes nearly 80 of them, likely reflecting Apple's use of AI models to help identify flaws and vulnerabilities. I expect future updates to ship with an increasing number of patches as well. It's not just Apple, either: Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update had a record 570 patches. Luckily, none of the flaws patched in iOS 26.6 were zero-days, so none were actively exploited or publicly disclosed before this update.

            Credit: Rene Ramos/Lifehacker
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game finished its second round last week. The game invites readers to make predictions on what products and features Apple may announce this year, all for the chance to win the latest Apple Watch. While we won't know the answers of these questions until Apple's September event, we do have the results. Check out what Lifehacker readers think Apple will announce this year, and come back Aug. 18 to participate in the final round.What will Apple call its foldable iPhone?  Apple is almost assuredly going to reveal its first foldable iPhone during WWDC this year. The major question left is, what will the company call it? Lifehacker asked readers to pick from the following four options: iPhone 18 Fold, iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra, or none of the above. While iPhone Ultra was the most popular name choice, with 30% of readers choosing it, slightly more respondents think Apple will go with another name. We'll see who is right in just over a month. 
If Apple announces a foldable iPhone, how much will it cost?Apple devices are notoriously expensive, and those prices are only continuing to rise. As such, it stands to reason that Apple's most complex and feature-filled iPhone yet will also be its priciest. Nearly a quarter of Lifehacker respondents believe the price will be somewhere between $1,000 and $1,499, while another near quarter think it'll cost $1,500 to $1,999. However, a whopping 41% believe it will cost more than $2,000. Personally, I think that's a good guess, considering the product and the current state of the market.  
Will Apple make the Dynamic Island smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro?The iPhone 18 Pro will likely take a backseat to Apple's foldable iPhone, and, as such, will likely be a small upgrade over the iPhone 17 Pro. Still, rumors speculate that Apple will shrink the size of the Dynamic Island on the 18 Pro, to make it a bit less pronounced when looking at the display. A little less than 43% of respondents don't buy that, while just over 57% believe it. While it'd be great to get as close to no camera cutout as possible, for a truly screen-only iPhone front, I find the Dynamic Island useful, and I'm not sure making it smaller would improve that. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Will the Apple Watch add body temperature tracking?While the Apple Watch Series 11 can detect wrist temperature, Apple is also upgrading the health sensors on its wearables. As such, it's possible the next generation of Apple Waches could read your body temperature as a whole, replacing the need for dedicated thermometers. While nearly 18% don't think that's coming, over 82% do.    Will Apple release new AirPods with cameras? One AirPods rumor that has persisted for years is that Apple is working on embedding cameras in its earbuds. While that might sound ridiculous, the concept actually makes sense: Apple would use these cameras not to take pictures, but to allow Siri AI to see the world around you. It could turn your AirPods into an AI device, and eliminate the need for you to take out your iPhone every time you want to ask the assistant a visual question. That said, most Lifehacker readers don't think Apple will do this, including over 68% of respondents. We'll just have to see what Apple decides to do.

title: How to Make Sure Your Claude Chats Don't Get Shared Publicly (Again)
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Shared Claude chats were exposed on Google over the weekend.
                                            At this time, it isn't possible to check if your chats were exposed, but you can prevent them from being shared in the future.
                                            It seems only shared Claude chats were affected in this case, so the solution is to delete those shared snapshots and disable the public links.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you use Claude, Anthropic's AI chatbot, you might be aware that your chats may have been exposed on Google. The news broke over the weekend, as Redditors discovered a treasure trove of conversations between Claude users and their AI bots. All one had to do was search for a keyword followed by "site:claude.ai/share" to find Claude conversations about that topic. It was, to be frank, quite the mess.Luckily, Anthropic quickly plugged the security hole. Ever since, searching Google with "site:claude.ai/share" returns no results, so you can't find any of these chats today if you try. However, it's not necessarily a huge comfort to know that Google indexed these conversations in the first place—and for the second time in a year, at that. Anthropic dealt with a similar situation back in September, and while it isn't alone—Google once also indexed ChatGPT conversations—you might understandably be concerned about future chats leaking onto the web, as well as wonder whether your current chats were exposed.   Why were Claude chats exposed?The thing is, it doesn't seem like every Claude chat had an equal risk of exposure here. Anthropic is adamant it doesn't share chat links to Google directly; instead, the vast majority (if not the entirety) of these chats appear to be conversations that individuals decided to share with others on the open web, according to Google. Claude lets you share your chats publicly if you wish, and while that can be convenient for showing friends, family, or colleagues a specific discussion, it might also open up your chat to Google's web crawlers, as when you share a chat, it generates a public link.
So, there's a silver lining in that private Claude chats that weren't shared are unlikely to be involved in this latest exposure. If you don't share your chats with anyone, you should be in the clear—though Futurism did report that one user in September's Claude debacle swears they never shared their exposed chats. However, if you do share Claude chats, your conversations might have been part of the indexing that happened over the weekend.Further complicating things, it seems that Claude's "artifacts" are still visible on Google. Claude generates artifacts when the content of your project meets certain criteria, and can include anything like documents, code snippets, HTML sites, SVG images, diagrams, flowcharts, and Interactive React components. In many cases, users may want these artifacts to be public, as they may be meant to be shared widely. However, if you don't want your artifacts indexed on Google, you'll have to take action. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to protect your Claude chats from future exposureWhile there doesn't appear to be any reliable way to identify whether your chats and artifacts were included in this exposure, you can ensure that none of them are ever indexed by a search engine in the future. To do so, you'll essentially have to shut down sharing. To start, head to Settings > Privacy in Claude, then choose "Manage" next to "Shared chats." Once this new page appears, you'll see all shared chats, including a link to the conversation and the date shared. From here, scroll through the list and select "Unshare" next to each chat you'd like to remove. This won't delete your chats; only their snapshots connected to these public links.
